background.authorship: The heading is simply לְדָוִד, ledavid; it does not contain the word “psalm.” The expression associates the poem with David. Its preposition can express authorship, belonging, or dedication, hence “by David,” “of David,” or “for David”; these possibilities do not carry equal weight in every historical interpretation. Jewish and Christian tradition generally understood David as its author. Albert Barnes explicitly accepts that attribution while acknowledging that the occasion cannot be recovered. Critical scholars distinguish the heading’s attribution from evidence about composition: Phil J. Botha reads the poem as a later work presenting David as an example for its readers, rather than necessarily recording David’s own words. Neither the first-person voice nor the heading independently establishes the historical author. [Barnes](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/26.htm); [Botha](https://repository.up.ac.za/handle/2263/16657).
background.setting: The text names an altar, God’s house, and worshiping assemblies. It asks for judgment and examination, rejects corrupt company, and pleads not to share violent people’s fate. It names no accusation, persecutor, king, war, or illness. Davidic interpretations place it around the early tenth century BCE and understand the sanctuary language in relation to a tent or earlier sanctuary, since Solomon’s temple would be later. Proposed connections with Saul’s pursuit or Absalom’s rebellion remain conjectural. A. F. Kirkpatrick reports Ewald’s alternative suggestion of a national calamity, perhaps pestilence, under Josiah in the late seventh century BCE, based on the fear of being swept away with others. Temple-based reconstructions include an accused worshiper seeking divine judgment, a pilgrim declaring fitness to enter, and a priest preparing for service; the testing, washing, and altar language supplies their basis. Richard Clifford favors priestly origins. Botha and Annette Potgieter instead emphasize literary instruction for a community after the exile; Potgieter proposes Persian-period composition or editing, approximately 539–332 BCE, from links with wisdom literature. These are reconstructions, not occasions stated by the poem. [Kirkpatrick](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/26.htm); [Potgieter](https://verbumetecclesia.org.za/index.php/ve/article/view/818/2063).
background.form: This is an individual prayer combining a declaration of integrity, requests for examination and rescue, confidence, and promised praise. Its classification varies with the proposed setting: prayer of innocence, individual lament, sanctuary entrance prayer, or instructional poem voiced as prayer. It is not an alphabetic acrostic and contains no Selah or musical direction. The heading belongs within verse 1 in the numbering supplied here. Paired clauses dominate. Verses 1 and 11 repeat walking in integrity; the opening refusal to falter answers the closing secure footing. Hands washed in innocence contrast with hands holding schemes and bribes. The evil assembly in verse 5 contrasts with the worshiping assemblies in verse 12. These repetitions form a frame rather than a fixed refrain. A 6/8 adaptation can preserve them, but may require additional lines or measures. The Masoretic accents mark phrasing and cantillation; they do not establish a recoverable 6/8 rhythm. Textual caution: the supplied verse 2 omits the third testing verb. Standard Masoretic editions include written צרופה with the reading צָרְפָה, from the root meaning to refine or test metal. [Masoretic text](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.26/).
background.themes: The speaker asks God to recognize integrity while also submitting the inner self to scrutiny. God’s loyal love and reliability ground the claim. Verses 4–5 describe refusal of corrupt fellowship; verses 6–8 turn toward cleansing, worship, thanksgiving, and love of God’s dwelling. Verses 9–10 ask that the speaker’s fate differ from that of violent, corrupt people. Verse 11 repeats the commitment to integrity alongside a request for redemption and grace. Verse 12 ends with firm footing and public blessing. The poem therefore joins ethical conduct, inward examination, sanctuary worship, and dependence on God. Its confidence and its appeal for mercy stand together; translation can preserve that tension without explaining it away.
background.reception: Rashi reads the claim to righteousness comparatively: David asks to be judged alongside the wicked, without claiming superiority to every righteous person. Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 107a reads verse 2 as David requesting a test before his failure involving Bathsheba; that is a later narrative interpretation, not information supplied by the psalm. Verse 8 appears in the Jewish Mah Tovu prayers associated with entering the synagogue. In Christian reception, Augustine hears the Church established in Christ speaking, and interprets the testing as exposure and purification of hidden faults. Verses 6–12 supplied the traditional Roman Mass’s Lavabo prayer; the Greek and Latin tradition’s language about washing among innocent people and loving the house’s beauty has consequently shaped Christian familiarity with these verses. This is Psalm 25 in standard Septuagint and Vulgate numbering. No explicit New Testament quotation of this psalm is generally identified. Pilate’s handwashing in Matthew 27:24 is a comparable innocence gesture, not a marked quotation. These uses matter for inherited wording, but do not determine the Hebrew’s meaning. [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16247/jewish/Chapter-26.htm); [Sanhedrin 107a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.107a); [Mah Tovu](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Ashkenaz,_Weekday,_Shacharit,_Preparatory_Prayers,_Ma_Tovu); [Augustine](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801026.htm); [Lavabo](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09044b.htm); [Matthew comparison](https://www.esv.org/Psalm+26:6;Psalm+73:13;Matthew+27:24/).

questions.question: Within the requested 6/8 target, will you give the paired clauses additional rhythmic space or compress them into shorter recurring units?
questions.background: The brief fixes a 6/8 target but supplies no tune or line template. Musical 6/8 normally groups six eighth notes into two main beats; it does not itself prescribe alternating six- and eight-syllable lines. Either implementation leaves choices about clause length, repetitions, and unstressed syllables. Verses 1–2 and 6–8 are especially resistant to compression.

options.choice: Spread complete parallel clauses across additional lines or measures while maintaining the chosen 6/8 pattern.
options.held_by: A strategy available for this commission, preserving the fuller clause structure represented by KJV and ASV; neither is itself a 6/8 version.
options.effect: Preserves the accumulating petitions, images, and repetitions; requires a longer setting and may carry syntax across musical boundaries.

options.choice: Compress paired clauses into shorter rhythmic units, retaining their central contrasts.
options.held_by: A strategy available for this commission, analogous to the compression in CEV, especially verses 4–7; CEV is not being identified as a 6/8 version.
options.effect: Produces more compact recurring units; may reduce the threefold testing, repeated movement words, or distinction between thanksgiving and recounting.

questions.question: Will the opening ask God to judge the speaker or explicitly to vindicate the speaker?
questions.background: שָׁפְטֵנִי, shofteni, asks God to exercise judgment. The following claim of integrity supports an expectation of favorable judgment, but that outcome is not separately stated in the imperative. The choice establishes whether the opening sounds like submission to examination or an appeal for justice.

options.choice: Retain the broader request to judge or give judgment.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NABRE also uses judgment language.
options.effect: Keeps the request open to scrutiny and connects closely with verse 2; modern readers may hear a request for condemnation.

options.choice: Make the desired favorable judgment explicit with vindication language.
options.effect: Clarifies the appeal for recognition of innocence; narrows the judicial verb to the outcome the speaker seeks.

questions.question: Will תֹּם emphasize personal integrity, sincere loyalty, or blameless conduct?
questions.background: בְּתֻמִּי recurs in both verses and describes soundness or completeness of conduct. It can support English language of integrity, sincerity, innocence, or blamelessness. The Hebrew does not add either a claim to universal sinlessness or an explicit limitation to one accusation. Verse 11 retains a plea for grace.

options.choice: Use integrity language consistently in both verses.
options.effect: Preserves the repeated ethical claim without specifying its exact scope; the abstract noun may be harder to fit into the meter.

options.choice: Express the claim through innocence or blameless conduct.
options.held_by: Brenton’s Septuagint uses innocence; NIV uses blameless-life language.
options.effect: Makes the claim concrete and forceful; English may make it sound more absolute than intended.

options.choice: Emphasize sincerity or undivided loyalty.
options.held_by: The Judaica Press translation accompanying Rashi uses sincerity in verse 1. [Judaica Press and Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16247/jewish/Chapter-26.htm)
options.effect: Foregrounds wholehearted commitment; can understate the claim about actual conduct.

questions.question: How will you represent YHWH throughout the psalm?
questions.background: YHWH is the only divine name used, occurring twice in verse 1 and once in verses 2, 6, 8, and 12. Elohim, Adonai, and Elyon do not occur. Adonai is the traditional Jewish spoken substitute, not an additional written name here. The alternatives have different syllable counts and stresses.

options.choice: Use LORD, with the typographic distinction retained where possible.
options.held_by: KJV and WEB; the Jewish reading tradition substitutes Adonai.
options.effect: Connects with familiar English worship and avoids pronouncing the name; listeners cannot hear the small-cap distinction.

options.choice: Use Jehovah consistently.
options.effect: Makes the proper name audible and follows an established English tradition; adds syllables and uses a historically mediated English form.

options.choice: Use Yahweh consistently.
options.effect: Distinguishes the personal name from a title in speech; changes familiar liturgical wording and the rhythmic footprint.

questions.question: Will the speaker chiefly recount past conduct and make future commitments, or describe an ongoing way of life?
questions.background: The Hebrew alternates completed-form verbs, including walking, trusting, refusing company, hating, and loving, with forms that can express continuing practice, intention, or future action. English tense cannot reproduce that range mechanically. Verse 11 has a Hebrew imperfect for walking, while the Septuagint presents past walking.

options.choice: Keep a marked movement from past conduct to future resolve and praise.
options.held_by: KJV, with past walking and trusting, future washing and walking, and future blessing.
options.effect: Gives the prayer a testimony-and-vow progression; may separate actions that could describe the same continuing practice.

options.choice: Use the present for established habits and commitments, reserving the future where context calls for it.
options.held_by: NET and, in several clauses, NRSVUE. [NET](https://search.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ps.26&version=NET%3BNIV)
options.effect: Presents a coherent current life before God; reduces the audible distinctions among the Hebrew verb forms.

questions.question: How will you retain and present לְדָוִד without claiming more about authorship than your wording intends?
questions.background: The heading contains David’s name with the preposition le-. It contains neither a genre label nor a historical occasion. Its presentation also affects whether it enters the metrical text or remains outside the sung lines.

options.choice: Print “Of David” as a separate heading outside the metrical lines.
options.held_by: NRSVUE uses this heading; KJV and ASV also retain the Davidic attribution.
options.effect: Preserves the received association with David while leaving its precise relationship less explicit; readers may still understand authorship.

options.choice: Print “By David” as a separate heading.
options.effect: Makes the traditional authorship interpretation clear; resolves a relationship that the Hebrew preposition alone does not spell out.

options.choice: Render the heading as a dedication or association with David and explain that interpretation in a note.
options.held_by: The association reading accords with critical approaches such as Botha’s David-as-model interpretation; it is not his proposed English heading.
options.effect: Allows a later Davidic literary voice; makes the translator’s historical interpretation more visible.

questions.question: How will you express the third examination request found in the standard Masoretic text: as testing or as refining?
questions.background: The supplied transcription jumps from וְנַסֵּנִי to כִלְיוֹתַי. Standard editions include written צרופה, read צָרְפָה, between them. This is a transcription issue, not evidence for an alternative two-request Hebrew text. The root evokes testing or refining metal; the Septuagint explicitly uses fire language. [Masoretic text](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.26/).

options.choice: Render the third verb as another request to test or assay the inner self.
options.effect: Keeps the focus on establishing genuineness and preserves three requests; the metalworking image becomes less apparent.

options.choice: Make refining or purification by fire explicit.
options.held_by: Judaica Press uses refining; Brenton’s Septuagint explicitly describes purification by fire. [Brenton](https://biblehub.com/sep/psalms/26.htm)
options.effect: Preserves the furnace image and its purifying possibilities; may suggest removal of impurity rather than primarily examination.

questions.question: Will you retain the bodily organs or express the inward faculties they represent?
questions.background: כִלְיוֹתַי וְלִבִּי means the speaker’s kidneys and heart. Together they expose the inward person to examination: desires, thought, conscience, and intention. Modern English distributes these functions differently and does not normally use kidneys this way.

options.choice: Keep kidneys and heart, with explanation outside the metrical text if needed.
options.held_by: The Hebrew text and the Greek Septuagint retain both organs; KJV’s older “reins” likewise denotes kidneys.
options.effect: Preserves the embodied imagery and two-part expression; can sound medical or obscure.

options.choice: Use heart and mind.
options.effect: Offers a familiar English pair and compact rhythm; substitutes modern associations and changes the bodily mapping.

options.choice: Name inward thoughts, desires, or motives.
options.held_by: NET uses thoughts and motives; GNT uses desires and thoughts.
options.effect: Clarifies the examination’s moral reach; replaces the concrete organs with interpretation.

questions.question: Will the handwashing remain a concrete act with moral significance, become an explicit innocence gesture, or follow the ancient reading about innocent companions?
questions.background: אֶרְחַץ בְּנִקָּיוֹן כַּפָּי joins washing the hands with innocence or cleanness. It can describe ritual action carrying an ethical claim or function as an image of conduct. The Greek and traditional Latin versions instead place the washing among innocent people. [Greek text](https://www.biblehub.com/sepd/psalms/26.htm).

options.choice: Keep washing the hands in innocence without explaining the relationship.
options.effect: Preserves ritual action and moral symbolism together; leaves English readers to interpret the unusual expression.

options.choice: Explain that the washing demonstrates innocence.
options.effect: Clarifies the gesture’s significance; resolves what the Hebrew leaves compressed.

options.choice: Follow the Greek and Latin tradition by placing the washing among innocent people.
options.held_by: Septuagint, traditional Vulgate, and Augustine’s exposition.
options.effect: Preserves a major liturgical reading and strengthens the fellowship contrast; changes the Hebrew abstract quality into a group of people.

questions.question: Will the speaker physically circle the altar or more generally approach it for worship?
questions.background: וַאֲסֹבְבָה אֶת־מִזְבַּחֲךָ uses a verb of going around or surrounding. A ritual circuit is a natural reading, but the exact ceremony is not identified. Some translations express the worshiping purpose rather than the movement.

options.choice: Retain movement around the altar.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use “compass”; WEB retains going about the altar.
options.effect: Keeps the spatial action and connection with walking; can suggest a specific procession whose details remain unknown.

options.choice: Express appearing or worshiping at the altar.
options.held_by: NET describes appearing before it; CEV describes worship there.
options.effect: Makes the action’s purpose clear and fits compact lines; loses the circular movement.

questions.question: Will the speaker make thanksgiving audible or come to hear it?
questions.background: The Masoretic לַשְׁמִעַ is a causative infinitive: to make heard. The Septuagint has an infinitive meaning to hear. The difference changes the speaker from a voice of thanksgiving to a listener joining worship. NABRE follows the hearing interpretation. [NABRE](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/psalms/26).

options.choice: Follow the Masoretic vocalization and make the speaker proclaim thanksgiving aloud.
options.effect: Preserves the causative verb and public testimony; excludes the listening role found in the Greek tradition.

options.choice: Follow the Greek tradition and make the speaker hear thanksgiving or praise.
options.effect: Emphasizes participation in an existing act of worship; departs from the Masoretic causative reading.

questions.question: Will the object of love be God’s dwelling or the beauty of God’s house?
questions.background: The Masoretic מְעוֹן בֵּיתֶךָ describes the dwelling or habitation of God’s house. The Septuagint instead speaks of its beauty or comeliness, followed by the traditional Latin version. This is a substantive ancient-version difference, not simply two English synonyms.

options.choice: Retain the dwelling or habitation reading.
options.effect: Keeps the Hebrew focus on God’s abode and its parallel with the following dwelling-place; may require smoothing a redundant English phrase.

options.choice: Use the beauty reading, identifying its Greek basis if notes are provided.
options.effect: Preserves familiar Greek and Latin worship language; introduces an aesthetic emphasis absent from the Masoretic noun.

questions.question: Will you retain male terms for the corrupt people or use descriptions that leave their gender unspecified?
questions.background: מְתֵי in verse 4 and אַנְשֵׁי in verse 9 are male human terms in these expressions. Other descriptions, such as sinners and wicked people, are grammatically masculine plurals that can designate groups more broadly. The speaker’s first-person forms do not themselves specify gender; the Davidic heading supplies a traditional male identity.

options.choice: Retain men where the Hebrew uses male human terms.
options.effect: Preserves the wording’s male social presentation; English may imply that only men are in view.

options.choice: Use people or substantival descriptions such as the deceitful and the bloodthirsty.
options.held_by: NRSVUE uses descriptions without male nouns in these places.
options.effect: Allows the ethical categories to include any gender; makes the source’s male vocabulary less visible.

questions.question: How consistently will you preserve walking, sitting, entering, and standing as images of conduct and belonging?
questions.background: Walking recurs in verses 1, 3, and 11; sitting with corrupt people recurs in verses 4–5; secure standing closes the poem. These movements connect moral conduct, chosen company, and security. English idioms can communicate the meanings while obscuring the network.

options.choice: Retain the recurring physical verbs wherever workable.
options.effect: Preserves the poem’s embodied links and framing; some expressions may sound less natural in English.

options.choice: Translate the movements into conduct, association, and safety where those meanings dominate.
options.effect: Makes the claims immediately understandable and can shorten lines; weakens the repeated imagery.

questions.question: Does the closing clause describe unwavering trust or confidence that the speaker will not fall?
questions.background: After בָּטַחְתִּי, I have trusted, comes לֹא אֶמְעָד, I shall not falter or slip. It can stand as an assurance following trust, or qualify the character of the trust. There is no explicit Hebrew equivalent of KJV’s supplied “therefore.”

options.choice: Make not falling a separate assurance resulting from trust.
options.held_by: KJV; the Septuagint also gives an emphatic assurance against being shaken.
options.effect: Connects the opening with the final secure footing; makes an inferred logical relationship explicit if a connective is supplied.

options.choice: Attach the clause to trusting and describe trust without wavering.
options.effect: Produces a compact description of steadfast faith; reduces the distinct prediction of security.

questions.question: Which aspect of חֶסֶד will your English foreground?
questions.background: חַסְדְּךָ refers to God’s dependable kindness or loyal love. English terms divide its affectionate, merciful, and relational dimensions. The Septuagint foregrounds mercy; the supplied English versions use lovingkindness.

options.choice: Use lovingkindness or steadfast-love language.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE uses steadfast-love language.
options.effect: Emphasizes enduring benevolence; may require more syllables and leave loyalty implicit.

options.choice: Use mercy or kindness.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton emphasize mercy; Judaica Press uses kindness.
options.effect: Provides familiar, shorter vocabulary; may underrepresent the enduring relational commitment.

options.choice: Emphasize faithfulness or loyal commitment.
options.held_by: NET foregrounds faithfulness in this clause.
options.effect: Makes reliability central and links with trust; reduces the warmth conveyed by love language.

questions.question: Will walking בַּאֲמִתֶּךָ mean living in God’s truth, being guided by God’s faithfulness, or acting faithfully toward God?
questions.background: אֱמֶת includes truth, reliability, and faithfulness. The suffix identifies a relation to God, but English must articulate how that quality governs the speaker’s conduct. NRSVUE explicitly offers divine faithfulness as an alternative to its wording about human faithfulness. The Greek replaces walking with language of pleasing or being pleased. [NRSVUE and note](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2026&version=NRSVUE).

options.choice: Retain walking in God’s truth.
options.effect: Preserves the source’s compressed relationship and walking image; truth may sound chiefly doctrinal to modern readers.

options.choice: Describe conduct guided or sustained by God’s faithfulness.
options.effect: Makes God’s reliability the setting for conduct; explains the preposition rather than leaving its relationship open.

options.choice: Describe the speaker as living faithfully toward God.
options.effect: Makes the ethical response clear; shifts the immediate emphasis toward the speaker’s loyalty.

options.choice: Follow the Greek tradition’s language of pleasing or delight in God’s truth.
options.held_by: Septuagint; Brenton presents the speaker as pleased with God’s truth.
options.effect: Preserves an ancient reading; loses this occurrence of the Hebrew walking motif.

questions.question: Will מְתֵי־שָׁוְא describe worthless company or people characterized by falsehood?
questions.background: שָׁוְא ranges across emptiness, worthlessness, unreality, and falsehood. The parallel description of concealed or deceptive people can favor falsehood, but does not remove the broader sense.

options.choice: Use language of vanity, emptiness, or worthlessness.
options.effect: Preserves the word’s broad judgment of futility; modern English can make it sound like a denial of people’s intrinsic worth.

options.choice: Identify the people as false or deceitful.
options.effect: Makes the ethical criticism precise and clear; narrows the Hebrew’s wider range.

questions.question: Will נַעֲלָמִים identify concealed wrongdoing, hypocrisy, or lawbreaking?
questions.background: The Hebrew participle comes from a root meaning to hide or be concealed. Calling these people hypocrites interprets what their concealment means. Rashi describes people acting secretly in darkness. The Septuagint instead identifies lawbreakers. [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16247/jewish/Chapter-26.htm).

options.choice: Keep the concealment visible by describing people who hide their actions.
options.effect: Preserves the unusual image and avoids specifying a public religious pretense; requires an explanatory phrase.

options.choice: Use dissemblers, pretenders, or hypocrites.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use dissemblers; WEB uses hypocrites.
options.effect: Gives an immediately recognizable moral category; identifies the nature of the concealment more specifically than the root itself.

options.choice: Use lawbreakers or transgressors, following the Greek tradition.
options.effect: Preserves an ancient interpretation; removes the Hebrew reference to concealment.

questions.question: Will you retain an explicit declaration of hatred or express its practical force as refusal of evil company?
questions.background: שָׂנֵאתִי is a strong verb of hating or detesting. Its immediate object is the assembly of evildoers. The next clause states refusal to sit with the wicked. Compressing both into avoidance changes the emotional force as well as the length.

options.choice: Retain hate or detest and keep its stated object.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE retains hatred of the company.
options.effect: Preserves the declaration’s intensity and its distinction from the following refusal; can sound more personally hostile in English.

options.choice: Express rejection chiefly through refusal to join evil company.
options.held_by: CEV compresses verses 4–5 into refusal of corrupt association. [CEV](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2026&version=CEV)
options.effect: Produces a compact behavioral statement suitable for constrained rhythm; loses the explicit emotional declaration.

questions.question: How will washing, movement around the altar, and thanksgiving relate syntactically?
questions.background: The altar verb is a cohortative joined with waw, allowing intention, purpose, or result after washing. Verse 7 then uses two infinitives introduced by le-, naturally expressing purpose. English versions also recast them as actions accompanying the movement.

options.choice: State washing and altar movement, then introduce thanksgiving and recounting as their purpose.
options.effect: Keeps the goal of the action explicit; produces a sentence extending across two verses.

options.choice: Make altar access the purpose or result of washing.
options.held_by: NET’s translation and grammatical note. [NET notes on verses 6–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+26%3A6-8&version=NET)
options.effect: Clarifies the cohortative’s possible force; states a relationship that simple coordination leaves implicit.

options.choice: Present thanksgiving and recounting as accompanying the movement.
options.effect: Creates a continuous worship scene and flexible metrical phrasing; makes purpose less explicit.

questions.question: Will you specify a thanksgiving song and miracles, or keep the broader language of voiced thanks and wondrous deeds?
questions.background: קוֹל תּוֹדָה is a voice or sound of thanksgiving; a song is possible in context but no separate word for song occurs. נִפְלְאוֹתֶיךָ denotes God’s wonderful things or deeds, without distinguishing modern categories of miracle and providence. כָּל, all, gives the recounting an expansive scope.

options.choice: Keep voiced thanksgiving and all God’s wondrous deeds without specifying a musical form or kind of wonder.
options.effect: Preserves the breadth and explicit totality; may be less immediately singable than a shorter familiar phrase.

options.choice: Make the musical performance explicit through a thanksgiving song.
options.effect: Creates a clear worship scene; supplies a musical form inferred from the context.

options.choice: Call the wonders miracles.
options.effect: Uses familiar concrete religious vocabulary; may narrow the deeds to extraordinary interventions.

questions.question: Will you preserve house and dwelling language or identify the location explicitly as the temple?
questions.background: בַּיִת means house; מָעוֹן and מִשְׁכָּן describe habitation or dwelling. The sanctuary setting is clear, but the verse does not use a separate architectural term identifying Solomon’s building. Rendering temple makes the institutional setting explicit.

options.choice: Keep house and dwelling language.
options.effect: Preserves the domestic imagery and leaves the sanctuary’s historical form open; can sound redundant in English.

options.choice: Identify the place as the temple or sanctuary.
options.held_by: NET and GNT make the temple setting explicit.
options.effect: Makes the worship location clear and can simplify the line; may suggest a specific building or period more strongly.

questions.question: Will כָּבוֹד be rendered as glory, splendor, honor, or an explicit manifestation of divine presence?
questions.background: כְּבוֹדֶךָ can evoke honor, majesty, or manifested divine glory. Its dwelling at the sanctuary encourages a presence-related reading, but the Hebrew does not separately say brightness or visible appearance.

options.choice: Use glory or honor without further explanation.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB use glory; KJV uses honor.
options.effect: Preserves the compact traditional term and its breadth; readers may understand reputation rather than divine presence.

options.choice: Express splendor or glorious presence explicitly.
options.held_by: NET foregrounds revealed splendor; NLT makes glorious presence explicit.
options.effect: Makes the sanctuary association vivid; adds interpretation and may imply visible radiance.

questions.question: Will the plea retain the gathering image or explicitly ask to be spared death with the wicked?
questions.background: אַל־תֶּאֱסֹף asks God not to gather up or take away the speaker’s life with sinners. The parallel reference to life and violent people supports a feared shared destruction. The Greek explicitly uses a verb of destroying together.

options.choice: Retain gathering or being swept away with sinners.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE uses sweeping-away language.
options.effect: Preserves the collective image and leaves the precise disaster unspecified; gathering can sound harmless without context.

options.choice: Make death or destruction explicit.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton; CEV explicitly names death.
options.effect: Clarifies the danger and the plea for a different fate; resolves an implication rather than reproducing the Hebrew image.

questions.question: Will נַפְשִׁי remain soul, or become me or my life alongside the parallel חַיָּי?
questions.background: נֶפֶשׁ can designate the living self or life, not necessarily a separable immaterial soul. It stands parallel here to חַיָּי, my life. English soul preserves traditional wording but can introduce a distinction between body and soul that the parallel does not require.

options.choice: Keep soul in the first clause and life in the second.
options.effect: Preserves two different source terms and familiar wording; may suggest two separately endangered parts of a person.

options.choice: Use me or my life for נַפְשִׁי.
options.held_by: NRSVUE and NET use the personal self in the first clause.
options.effect: Makes the whole person’s survival clear; reduces lexical distinction between the parallel clauses.

questions.question: Will אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים emphasize bloodshed already committed, a violent character, or bloodthirstiness?
questions.background: The expression literally describes men of bloods, an idiom associated with bloodshed and bloodguilt. English descriptions differ over whether they identify acts, guilt, or disposition.

options.choice: Retain the blood image through men of blood or bloodstained people.
options.held_by: ASV retains men of blood; KJV uses the older expression bloody men.
options.effect: Keeps the image and potential association with guilt; requires readers to understand the idiom.

options.choice: Use violent people or murderers.
options.held_by: NET uses violence language; GNT identifies murderers.
options.effect: Makes the conduct clear; murderers narrows the category to completed killing, while violent people broadens it.

options.choice: Use bloodthirsty people.
options.effect: Preserves a vivid blood-related expression; foregrounds appetite or disposition rather than bloodguilt.

questions.question: Will זִמָּה describe wickedness generally or deliberate evil planning?
questions.background: זִמָּה can denote a plan or purpose and, in condemnatory contexts, an evil scheme or wickedness. Here it is located in the offenders’ hands, combining intention with capacity for action. Nothing in the verse requires its more specialized sexual uses elsewhere.

options.choice: Use a broad term such as wickedness or mischief.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB use wickedness; KJV uses mischief.
options.effect: Keeps the charge broad and compact; may understate deliberation, and modern mischief can sound trivial.

options.choice: Identify evil plans, devices, or schemes.
options.effect: Makes deliberate corruption clear; interprets the term more specifically as planning.

questions.question: Will you leave the bribes in their hands unexplained, or identify whether they give or receive them?
questions.background: וִימִינָם מָלְאָה שֹּׁחַד says their right hand is full of a bribe or bribery. The image does not expressly identify the direction of the transaction. English versions divide between people ready to offer bribes and people who take them. [Translation comparison](https://search.biblegateway.com/verse/en/Psalm%2026%3A10).

options.choice: Retain the right hand full of bribes without specifying the transaction.
options.effect: Preserves the ambiguity and the contrast with the speaker’s washed hands; leaves the social role unstated.

options.choice: Identify people offering bribes.
options.effect: Makes corrupt attempts to influence others explicit; excludes the receiving interpretation.

options.choice: Identify people taking bribes.
options.effect: Makes corrupt acceptance of payment explicit; excludes the offering interpretation.

questions.question: Will פְּדֵנִי retain redemption language or become an immediate request for rescue?
questions.background: The verb פּדה concerns release or redemption, including release from danger. This verse specifies neither a payment nor its means. Traditional Christian reception can hear ransom theology here, but that is not separately stated in the Hebrew.

options.choice: Retain redeem.
options.effect: Preserves the traditional term and release associations; may evoke a developed theological account or imply a payment.

options.choice: Use rescue or deliver.
options.held_by: NET uses rescue; Brenton uses redeem in his psalm text, while Augustine’s exposition discusses deliverance.
options.effect: Makes the immediate plea clear and can ease the meter; reduces the distinctive redemption vocabulary.

questions.question: Will וְחָנֵּנִי ask for gracious favor or mercy?
questions.background: The root חנן asks for favor freely shown to someone in need. Mercy is an established contextual rendering, but modern English can make it chiefly a request for forgiveness of wrongdoing. The verse itself does not confess a particular offense.

options.choice: Ask God to be gracious or show favor.
options.effect: Preserves the appeal to freely given help; gracious can sound formal or merely courteous.

options.choice: Ask God to have mercy.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB, and the Greek tradition.
options.effect: Retains familiar prayer language and emotional urgency; may lead readers to hear an unstated confession of guilt.

questions.question: Will the closing footing remain a physical image, become explicit safety, or emphasize uprightness?
questions.background: רַגְלִי עָמְדָה בְמִישׁוֹר describes the speaker’s foot as standing on level ground. מִישׁוֹר can also carry associations of straightness or equity; the Greek uses uprightness language. The completed-form verb can describe a presently established position. English may retain singular foot, use feet idiomatically, or speak of footing.

options.choice: Keep the foot or feet standing on level ground.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NIV uses plural feet.
options.effect: Preserves the image and answer to possible slipping in verse 1; leaves safety and moral straightness implicit.

options.choice: State that the speaker is secure or safe.
options.effect: Makes the assurance immediately clear; loses the foot and ground imagery.

options.choice: Make uprightness prominent.
options.held_by: The Septuagint’s wording and Augustine’s moral interpretation.
options.effect: Echoes the ethical claim of integrity; can weaken the sense of protection from falling.

questions.question: Will you retain the contrast between an evil assembly and worshiping assemblies, including the final plural?
questions.background: Verse 5 has קְהַל, an assembly; verse 12 has בְּמַקְהֵלִים, in assemblies, from the same root. Some English versions retain the plural; others express a single great congregation or the worshipers themselves. Great is not separately written in the Masoretic phrase.

options.choice: Use related assembly terms in both verses and retain the final plural.
options.effect: Preserves the word-family echo and repeated public worship; plural assemblies can sound institutional or geographically dispersed.

options.choice: Describe evil company in verse 5 and a single congregation in verse 12.
options.effect: Creates a readily imagined contrast in belonging; obscures the shared root and interprets the Hebrew plural collectively.

options.choice: Refer directly to worshipers or God’s gathered people.
options.effect: Clarifies who participates and can suit a shorter line; replaces the gathering noun and its lexical echo.

questions.question: Will the final line bless YHWH in the third person or address God directly in praise?
questions.background: The Masoretic אֲבָרֵךְ יְהוָה has YHWH as the object of blessing, without a second-person pronoun. The Septuagint includes an explicit you and treats Lord as an address. English bless can preserve the traditional verb, while praise makes its human-to-God function clearer.

options.choice: Retain a promise to bless YHWH.
options.effect: Preserves the Hebrew construction and traditional worship verb; modern listeners may associate blessing chiefly with receiving benefits.

options.choice: Use praise with YHWH as its object.
options.effect: Clarifies the act of worship; loses the distinctive blessing vocabulary.

options.choice: Address God directly with a promise to bless or praise you.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton retain direct address; CEV also closes by addressing God.
options.effect: Maintains direct prayer through the final words; follows the Greek construction rather than the Masoretic wording.

question.question: Within the requested 6/8 target, will you give the paired clauses additional rhythmic space or compress them into shorter recurring units?
question.background: The brief fixes a 6/8 target but supplies no tune or line template. Musical 6/8 normally groups six eighth notes into two main beats; it does not itself prescribe alternating six- and eight-syllable lines. Either implementation leaves choices about clause length, repetitions, and unstressed syllables. Verses 1–2 and 6–8 are especially resistant to compression.

options.choice: Spread complete parallel clauses across additional lines or measures while maintaining the chosen 6/8 pattern.
options.held_by: A strategy available for this commission, preserving the fuller clause structure represented by KJV and ASV; neither is itself a 6/8 version.
options.effect: Preserves the accumulating petitions, images, and repetitions; requires a longer setting and may carry syntax across musical boundaries.

options.choice: Compress paired clauses into shorter rhythmic units, retaining their central contrasts.
options.held_by: A strategy available for this commission, analogous to the compression in CEV, especially verses 4–7; CEV is not being identified as a 6/8 version.
options.effect: Produces more compact recurring units; may reduce the threefold testing, repeated movement words, or distinction between thanksgiving and recounting.

annotations.answer: Spread complete parallel clauses across additional lines or measures while maintaining the chosen 6/8 pattern.

question.question: Will the opening ask God to judge the speaker or explicitly to vindicate the speaker?
question.background: שָׁפְטֵנִי, shofteni, asks God to exercise judgment. The following claim of integrity supports an expectation of favorable judgment, but that outcome is not separately stated in the imperative. The choice establishes whether the opening sounds like submission to examination or an appeal for justice.

options.choice: Retain the broader request to judge or give judgment.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NABRE also uses judgment language.
options.effect: Keeps the request open to scrutiny and connects closely with verse 2; modern readers may hear a request for condemnation.

options.choice: Make the desired favorable judgment explicit with vindication language.
options.effect: Clarifies the appeal for recognition of innocence; narrows the judicial verb to the outcome the speaker seeks.

annotations.answer: Retain the broader request to judge or give judgment.

question.question: Will תֹּם emphasize personal integrity, sincere loyalty, or blameless conduct?
question.background: בְּתֻמִּי recurs in both verses and describes soundness or completeness of conduct. It can support English language of integrity, sincerity, innocence, or blamelessness. The Hebrew does not add either a claim to universal sinlessness or an explicit limitation to one accusation. Verse 11 retains a plea for grace.

options.choice: Use integrity language consistently in both verses.
options.effect: Preserves the repeated ethical claim without specifying its exact scope; the abstract noun may be harder to fit into the meter.

options.choice: Express the claim through innocence or blameless conduct.
options.held_by: Brenton’s Septuagint uses innocence; NIV uses blameless-life language.
options.effect: Makes the claim concrete and forceful; English may make it sound more absolute than intended.

options.choice: Emphasize sincerity or undivided loyalty.
options.held_by: The Judaica Press translation accompanying Rashi uses sincerity in verse 1. [Judaica Press and Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16247/jewish/Chapter-26.htm)
options.effect: Foregrounds wholehearted commitment; can understate the claim about actual conduct.

annotations.answer: Express the claim through innocence or blameless conduct.

question.question: How will you represent YHWH throughout the psalm?
question.background: YHWH is the only divine name used, occurring twice in verse 1 and once in verses 2, 6, 8, and 12. Elohim, Adonai, and Elyon do not occur. Adonai is the traditional Jewish spoken substitute, not an additional written name here. The alternatives have different syllable counts and stresses.

options.choice: Use LORD, with the typographic distinction retained where possible.
options.held_by: KJV and WEB; the Jewish reading tradition substitutes Adonai.
options.effect: Connects with familiar English worship and avoids pronouncing the name; listeners cannot hear the small-cap distinction.

options.choice: Use Jehovah consistently.
options.effect: Makes the proper name audible and follows an established English tradition; adds syllables and uses a historically mediated English form.

options.choice: Use Yahweh consistently.
options.effect: Distinguishes the personal name from a title in speech; changes familiar liturgical wording and the rhythmic footprint.

annotations.answer: Use LORD, with the typographic distinction retained where possible.

question.question: Will the speaker chiefly recount past conduct and make future commitments, or describe an ongoing way of life?
question.background: The Hebrew alternates completed-form verbs, including walking, trusting, refusing company, hating, and loving, with forms that can express continuing practice, intention, or future action. English tense cannot reproduce that range mechanically. Verse 11 has a Hebrew imperfect for walking, while the Septuagint presents past walking.

options.choice: Keep a marked movement from past conduct to future resolve and praise.
options.held_by: KJV, with past walking and trusting, future washing and walking, and future blessing.
options.effect: Gives the prayer a testimony-and-vow progression; may separate actions that could describe the same continuing practice.

options.choice: Use the present for established habits and commitments, reserving the future where context calls for it.
options.held_by: NET and, in several clauses, NRSVUE. [NET](https://search.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ps.26&version=NET%3BNIV)
options.effect: Presents a coherent current life before God; reduces the audible distinctions among the Hebrew verb forms.

annotations.answer: Use the present for established habits and commitments, reserving the future where context calls for it.

question.question: How will you retain and present לְדָוִד without claiming more about authorship than your wording intends?
question.background: The heading contains David’s name with the preposition le-. It contains neither a genre label nor a historical occasion. Its presentation also affects whether it enters the metrical text or remains outside the sung lines.

options.choice: Print “Of David” as a separate heading outside the metrical lines.
options.held_by: NRSVUE uses this heading; KJV and ASV also retain the Davidic attribution.
options.effect: Preserves the received association with David while leaving its precise relationship less explicit; readers may still understand authorship.

options.choice: Print “By David” as a separate heading.
options.effect: Makes the traditional authorship interpretation clear; resolves a relationship that the Hebrew preposition alone does not spell out.

options.choice: Render the heading as a dedication or association with David and explain that interpretation in a note.
options.held_by: The association reading accords with critical approaches such as Botha’s David-as-model interpretation; it is not his proposed English heading.
options.effect: Allows a later Davidic literary voice; makes the translator’s historical interpretation more visible.

annotations.answer: Print “Of David” as a separate heading outside the metrical lines.

question.question: How will you express the third examination request found in the standard Masoretic text: as testing or as refining?
question.background: The supplied transcription jumps from וְנַסֵּנִי to כִלְיוֹתַי. Standard editions include written צרופה, read צָרְפָה, between them. This is a transcription issue, not evidence for an alternative two-request Hebrew text. The root evokes testing or refining metal; the Septuagint explicitly uses fire language. [Masoretic text](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.26/).

options.choice: Render the third verb as another request to test or assay the inner self.
options.effect: Keeps the focus on establishing genuineness and preserves three requests; the metalworking image becomes less apparent.

options.choice: Make refining or purification by fire explicit.
options.held_by: Judaica Press uses refining; Brenton’s Septuagint explicitly describes purification by fire. [Brenton](https://biblehub.com/sep/psalms/26.htm)
options.effect: Preserves the furnace image and its purifying possibilities; may suggest removal of impurity rather than primarily examination.

annotations.answer: Make refining or purification by fire explicit.

question.question: Will you retain the bodily organs or express the inward faculties they represent?
question.background: כִלְיוֹתַי וְלִבִּי means the speaker’s kidneys and heart. Together they expose the inward person to examination: desires, thought, conscience, and intention. Modern English distributes these functions differently and does not normally use kidneys this way.

options.choice: Keep kidneys and heart, with explanation outside the metrical text if needed.
options.held_by: The Hebrew text and the Greek Septuagint retain both organs; KJV’s older “reins” likewise denotes kidneys.
options.effect: Preserves the embodied imagery and two-part expression; can sound medical or obscure.

options.choice: Use heart and mind.
options.effect: Offers a familiar English pair and compact rhythm; substitutes modern associations and changes the bodily mapping.

options.choice: Name inward thoughts, desires, or motives.
options.held_by: NET uses thoughts and motives; GNT uses desires and thoughts.
options.effect: Clarifies the examination’s moral reach; replaces the concrete organs with interpretation.

annotations.answer: Name inward thoughts, desires, or motives.

question.question: Will the handwashing remain a concrete act with moral significance, become an explicit innocence gesture, or follow the ancient reading about innocent companions?
question.background: אֶרְחַץ בְּנִקָּיוֹן כַּפָּי joins washing the hands with innocence or cleanness. It can describe ritual action carrying an ethical claim or function as an image of conduct. The Greek and traditional Latin versions instead place the washing among innocent people. [Greek text](https://www.biblehub.com/sepd/psalms/26.htm).

options.choice: Keep washing the hands in innocence without explaining the relationship.
options.effect: Preserves ritual action and moral symbolism together; leaves English readers to interpret the unusual expression.

options.choice: Explain that the washing demonstrates innocence.
options.effect: Clarifies the gesture’s significance; resolves what the Hebrew leaves compressed.

options.choice: Follow the Greek and Latin tradition by placing the washing among innocent people.
options.held_by: Septuagint, traditional Vulgate, and Augustine’s exposition.
options.effect: Preserves a major liturgical reading and strengthens the fellowship contrast; changes the Hebrew abstract quality into a group of people.

annotations.answer: Follow the Greek and Latin tradition by placing the washing among innocent people.

question.question: Will the speaker physically circle the altar or more generally approach it for worship?
question.background: וַאֲסֹבְבָה אֶת־מִזְבַּחֲךָ uses a verb of going around or surrounding. A ritual circuit is a natural reading, but the exact ceremony is not identified. Some translations express the worshiping purpose rather than the movement.

options.choice: Retain movement around the altar.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use “compass”; WEB retains going about the altar.
options.effect: Keeps the spatial action and connection with walking; can suggest a specific procession whose details remain unknown.

options.choice: Express appearing or worshiping at the altar.
options.held_by: NET describes appearing before it; CEV describes worship there.
options.effect: Makes the action’s purpose clear and fits compact lines; loses the circular movement.

annotations.answer: Retain movement around the altar.

question.question: Will the speaker make thanksgiving audible or come to hear it?
question.background: The Masoretic לַשְׁמִעַ is a causative infinitive: to make heard. The Septuagint has an infinitive meaning to hear. The difference changes the speaker from a voice of thanksgiving to a listener joining worship. NABRE follows the hearing interpretation. [NABRE](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/psalms/26).

options.choice: Follow the Masoretic vocalization and make the speaker proclaim thanksgiving aloud.
options.effect: Preserves the causative verb and public testimony; excludes the listening role found in the Greek tradition.

options.choice: Follow the Greek tradition and make the speaker hear thanksgiving or praise.
options.effect: Emphasizes participation in an existing act of worship; departs from the Masoretic causative reading.

annotations.answer: Follow the Greek tradition and make the speaker hear thanksgiving or praise.

question.question: Will the object of love be God’s dwelling or the beauty of God’s house?
question.background: The Masoretic מְעוֹן בֵּיתֶךָ describes the dwelling or habitation of God’s house. The Septuagint instead speaks of its beauty or comeliness, followed by the traditional Latin version. This is a substantive ancient-version difference, not simply two English synonyms.

options.choice: Retain the dwelling or habitation reading.
options.effect: Keeps the Hebrew focus on God’s abode and its parallel with the following dwelling-place; may require smoothing a redundant English phrase.

options.choice: Use the beauty reading, identifying its Greek basis if notes are provided.
options.effect: Preserves familiar Greek and Latin worship language; introduces an aesthetic emphasis absent from the Masoretic noun.

annotations.answer: Use the beauty reading, identifying its Greek basis if notes are provided.

question.question: Will you retain male terms for the corrupt people or use descriptions that leave their gender unspecified?
question.background: מְתֵי in verse 4 and אַנְשֵׁי in verse 9 are male human terms in these expressions. Other descriptions, such as sinners and wicked people, are grammatically masculine plurals that can designate groups more broadly. The speaker’s first-person forms do not themselves specify gender; the Davidic heading supplies a traditional male identity.

options.choice: Retain men where the Hebrew uses male human terms.
options.effect: Preserves the wording’s male social presentation; English may imply that only men are in view.

options.choice: Use people or substantival descriptions such as the deceitful and the bloodthirsty.
options.held_by: NRSVUE uses descriptions without male nouns in these places.
options.effect: Allows the ethical categories to include any gender; makes the source’s male vocabulary less visible.

annotations.answer: Retain men where the Hebrew uses male human terms.

question.question: How consistently will you preserve walking, sitting, entering, and standing as images of conduct and belonging?
question.background: Walking recurs in verses 1, 3, and 11; sitting with corrupt people recurs in verses 4–5; secure standing closes the poem. These movements connect moral conduct, chosen company, and security. English idioms can communicate the meanings while obscuring the network.

options.choice: Retain the recurring physical verbs wherever workable.
options.effect: Preserves the poem’s embodied links and framing; some expressions may sound less natural in English.

options.choice: Translate the movements into conduct, association, and safety where those meanings dominate.
options.effect: Makes the claims immediately understandable and can shorten lines; weakens the repeated imagery.

annotations.answer: Retain the recurring physical verbs wherever workable.

question.question: Does the closing clause describe unwavering trust or confidence that the speaker will not fall?
question.background: After בָּטַחְתִּי, I have trusted, comes לֹא אֶמְעָד, I shall not falter or slip. It can stand as an assurance following trust, or qualify the character of the trust. There is no explicit Hebrew equivalent of KJV’s supplied “therefore.”

options.choice: Make not falling a separate assurance resulting from trust.
options.held_by: KJV; the Septuagint also gives an emphatic assurance against being shaken.
options.effect: Connects the opening with the final secure footing; makes an inferred logical relationship explicit if a connective is supplied.

options.choice: Attach the clause to trusting and describe trust without wavering.
options.effect: Produces a compact description of steadfast faith; reduces the distinct prediction of security.

annotations.answer: Attach the clause to trusting and describe trust without wavering.

question.question: Which aspect of חֶסֶד will your English foreground?
question.background: חַסְדְּךָ refers to God’s dependable kindness or loyal love. English terms divide its affectionate, merciful, and relational dimensions. The Septuagint foregrounds mercy; the supplied English versions use lovingkindness.

options.choice: Use lovingkindness or steadfast-love language.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE uses steadfast-love language.
options.effect: Emphasizes enduring benevolence; may require more syllables and leave loyalty implicit.

options.choice: Use mercy or kindness.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton emphasize mercy; Judaica Press uses kindness.
options.effect: Provides familiar, shorter vocabulary; may underrepresent the enduring relational commitment.

options.choice: Emphasize faithfulness or loyal commitment.
options.held_by: NET foregrounds faithfulness in this clause.
options.effect: Makes reliability central and links with trust; reduces the warmth conveyed by love language.

annotations.answer: Emphasize faithfulness or loyal commitment.

question.question: Will walking בַּאֲמִתֶּךָ mean living in God’s truth, being guided by God’s faithfulness, or acting faithfully toward God?
question.background: אֱמֶת includes truth, reliability, and faithfulness. The suffix identifies a relation to God, but English must articulate how that quality governs the speaker’s conduct. NRSVUE explicitly offers divine faithfulness as an alternative to its wording about human faithfulness. The Greek replaces walking with language of pleasing or being pleased. [NRSVUE and note](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2026&version=NRSVUE).

options.choice: Retain walking in God’s truth.
options.effect: Preserves the source’s compressed relationship and walking image; truth may sound chiefly doctrinal to modern readers.

options.choice: Describe conduct guided or sustained by God’s faithfulness.
options.effect: Makes God’s reliability the setting for conduct; explains the preposition rather than leaving its relationship open.

options.choice: Describe the speaker as living faithfully toward God.
options.effect: Makes the ethical response clear; shifts the immediate emphasis toward the speaker’s loyalty.

options.choice: Follow the Greek tradition’s language of pleasing or delight in God’s truth.
options.held_by: Septuagint; Brenton presents the speaker as pleased with God’s truth.
options.effect: Preserves an ancient reading; loses this occurrence of the Hebrew walking motif.

annotations.answer: Follow the Greek tradition’s language of pleasing or delight in God’s truth.

question.question: Will מְתֵי־שָׁוְא describe worthless company or people characterized by falsehood?
question.background: שָׁוְא ranges across emptiness, worthlessness, unreality, and falsehood. The parallel description of concealed or deceptive people can favor falsehood, but does not remove the broader sense.

options.choice: Use language of vanity, emptiness, or worthlessness.
options.effect: Preserves the word’s broad judgment of futility; modern English can make it sound like a denial of people’s intrinsic worth.

options.choice: Identify the people as false or deceitful.
options.effect: Makes the ethical criticism precise and clear; narrows the Hebrew’s wider range.

annotations.answer: Identify the people as false or deceitful.

question.question: Will נַעֲלָמִים identify concealed wrongdoing, hypocrisy, or lawbreaking?
question.background: The Hebrew participle comes from a root meaning to hide or be concealed. Calling these people hypocrites interprets what their concealment means. Rashi describes people acting secretly in darkness. The Septuagint instead identifies lawbreakers. [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16247/jewish/Chapter-26.htm).

options.choice: Keep the concealment visible by describing people who hide their actions.
options.effect: Preserves the unusual image and avoids specifying a public religious pretense; requires an explanatory phrase.

options.choice: Use dissemblers, pretenders, or hypocrites.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use dissemblers; WEB uses hypocrites.
options.effect: Gives an immediately recognizable moral category; identifies the nature of the concealment more specifically than the root itself.

options.choice: Use lawbreakers or transgressors, following the Greek tradition.
options.effect: Preserves an ancient interpretation; removes the Hebrew reference to concealment.

annotations.answer: Use dissemblers, pretenders, or hypocrites.

question.question: Will you retain an explicit declaration of hatred or express its practical force as refusal of evil company?
question.background: שָׂנֵאתִי is a strong verb of hating or detesting. Its immediate object is the assembly of evildoers. The next clause states refusal to sit with the wicked. Compressing both into avoidance changes the emotional force as well as the length.

options.choice: Retain hate or detest and keep its stated object.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE retains hatred of the company.
options.effect: Preserves the declaration’s intensity and its distinction from the following refusal; can sound more personally hostile in English.

options.choice: Express rejection chiefly through refusal to join evil company.
options.held_by: CEV compresses verses 4–5 into refusal of corrupt association. [CEV](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2026&version=CEV)
options.effect: Produces a compact behavioral statement suitable for constrained rhythm; loses the explicit emotional declaration.

annotations.answer: Retain hate or detest and keep its stated object.

question.question: How will washing, movement around the altar, and thanksgiving relate syntactically?
question.background: The altar verb is a cohortative joined with waw, allowing intention, purpose, or result after washing. Verse 7 then uses two infinitives introduced by le-, naturally expressing purpose. English versions also recast them as actions accompanying the movement.

options.choice: State washing and altar movement, then introduce thanksgiving and recounting as their purpose.
options.effect: Keeps the goal of the action explicit; produces a sentence extending across two verses.

options.choice: Make altar access the purpose or result of washing.
options.held_by: NET’s translation and grammatical note. [NET notes on verses 6–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+26%3A6-8&version=NET)
options.effect: Clarifies the cohortative’s possible force; states a relationship that simple coordination leaves implicit.

options.choice: Present thanksgiving and recounting as accompanying the movement.
options.effect: Creates a continuous worship scene and flexible metrical phrasing; makes purpose less explicit.

annotations.answer: State washing and altar movement, then introduce thanksgiving and recounting as their purpose.

question.question: Will you specify a thanksgiving song and miracles, or keep the broader language of voiced thanks and wondrous deeds?
question.background: קוֹל תּוֹדָה is a voice or sound of thanksgiving; a song is possible in context but no separate word for song occurs. נִפְלְאוֹתֶיךָ denotes God’s wonderful things or deeds, without distinguishing modern categories of miracle and providence. כָּל, all, gives the recounting an expansive scope.

options.choice: Keep voiced thanksgiving and all God’s wondrous deeds without specifying a musical form or kind of wonder.
options.effect: Preserves the breadth and explicit totality; may be less immediately singable than a shorter familiar phrase.

options.choice: Make the musical performance explicit through a thanksgiving song.
options.effect: Creates a clear worship scene; supplies a musical form inferred from the context.

options.choice: Call the wonders miracles.
options.effect: Uses familiar concrete religious vocabulary; may narrow the deeds to extraordinary interventions.

annotations.answer: Make the musical performance explicit through a thanksgiving song.

question.question: Will you preserve house and dwelling language or identify the location explicitly as the temple?
question.background: בַּיִת means house; מָעוֹן and מִשְׁכָּן describe habitation or dwelling. The sanctuary setting is clear, but the verse does not use a separate architectural term identifying Solomon’s building. Rendering temple makes the institutional setting explicit.

options.choice: Keep house and dwelling language.
options.effect: Preserves the domestic imagery and leaves the sanctuary’s historical form open; can sound redundant in English.

options.choice: Identify the place as the temple or sanctuary.
options.held_by: NET and GNT make the temple setting explicit.
options.effect: Makes the worship location clear and can simplify the line; may suggest a specific building or period more strongly.

annotations.answer: Identify the place as the temple or sanctuary.

question.question: Will כָּבוֹד be rendered as glory, splendor, honor, or an explicit manifestation of divine presence?
question.background: כְּבוֹדֶךָ can evoke honor, majesty, or manifested divine glory. Its dwelling at the sanctuary encourages a presence-related reading, but the Hebrew does not separately say brightness or visible appearance.

options.choice: Use glory or honor without further explanation.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB use glory; KJV uses honor.
options.effect: Preserves the compact traditional term and its breadth; readers may understand reputation rather than divine presence.

options.choice: Express splendor or glorious presence explicitly.
options.held_by: NET foregrounds revealed splendor; NLT makes glorious presence explicit.
options.effect: Makes the sanctuary association vivid; adds interpretation and may imply visible radiance.

annotations.answer: Express splendor or glorious presence explicitly.

question.question: Will the plea retain the gathering image or explicitly ask to be spared death with the wicked?
question.background: אַל־תֶּאֱסֹף asks God not to gather up or take away the speaker’s life with sinners. The parallel reference to life and violent people supports a feared shared destruction. The Greek explicitly uses a verb of destroying together.

options.choice: Retain gathering or being swept away with sinners.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NRSVUE uses sweeping-away language.
options.effect: Preserves the collective image and leaves the precise disaster unspecified; gathering can sound harmless without context.

options.choice: Make death or destruction explicit.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton; CEV explicitly names death.
options.effect: Clarifies the danger and the plea for a different fate; resolves an implication rather than reproducing the Hebrew image.

annotations.answer: Make death or destruction explicit.

question.question: Will נַפְשִׁי remain soul, or become me or my life alongside the parallel חַיָּי?
question.background: נֶפֶשׁ can designate the living self or life, not necessarily a separable immaterial soul. It stands parallel here to חַיָּי, my life. English soul preserves traditional wording but can introduce a distinction between body and soul that the parallel does not require.

options.choice: Keep soul in the first clause and life in the second.
options.effect: Preserves two different source terms and familiar wording; may suggest two separately endangered parts of a person.

options.choice: Use me or my life for נַפְשִׁי.
options.held_by: NRSVUE and NET use the personal self in the first clause.
options.effect: Makes the whole person’s survival clear; reduces lexical distinction between the parallel clauses.

annotations.answer: Keep soul in the first clause and life in the second.

question.question: Will אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים emphasize bloodshed already committed, a violent character, or bloodthirstiness?
question.background: The expression literally describes men of bloods, an idiom associated with bloodshed and bloodguilt. English descriptions differ over whether they identify acts, guilt, or disposition.

options.choice: Retain the blood image through men of blood or bloodstained people.
options.held_by: ASV retains men of blood; KJV uses the older expression bloody men.
options.effect: Keeps the image and potential association with guilt; requires readers to understand the idiom.

options.choice: Use violent people or murderers.
options.held_by: NET uses violence language; GNT identifies murderers.
options.effect: Makes the conduct clear; murderers narrows the category to completed killing, while violent people broadens it.

options.choice: Use bloodthirsty people.
options.effect: Preserves a vivid blood-related expression; foregrounds appetite or disposition rather than bloodguilt.

annotations.answer: Use bloodthirsty people.

question.question: Will זִמָּה describe wickedness generally or deliberate evil planning?
question.background: זִמָּה can denote a plan or purpose and, in condemnatory contexts, an evil scheme or wickedness. Here it is located in the offenders’ hands, combining intention with capacity for action. Nothing in the verse requires its more specialized sexual uses elsewhere.

options.choice: Use a broad term such as wickedness or mischief.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB use wickedness; KJV uses mischief.
options.effect: Keeps the charge broad and compact; may understate deliberation, and modern mischief can sound trivial.

options.choice: Identify evil plans, devices, or schemes.
options.effect: Makes deliberate corruption clear; interprets the term more specifically as planning.

annotations.answer: Identify evil plans, devices, or schemes.

question.question: Will you leave the bribes in their hands unexplained, or identify whether they give or receive them?
question.background: וִימִינָם מָלְאָה שֹּׁחַד says their right hand is full of a bribe or bribery. The image does not expressly identify the direction of the transaction. English versions divide between people ready to offer bribes and people who take them. [Translation comparison](https://search.biblegateway.com/verse/en/Psalm%2026%3A10).

options.choice: Retain the right hand full of bribes without specifying the transaction.
options.effect: Preserves the ambiguity and the contrast with the speaker’s washed hands; leaves the social role unstated.

options.choice: Identify people offering bribes.
options.effect: Makes corrupt attempts to influence others explicit; excludes the receiving interpretation.

options.choice: Identify people taking bribes.
options.effect: Makes corrupt acceptance of payment explicit; excludes the offering interpretation.

annotations.answer: Retain the right hand full of bribes without specifying the transaction.

question.question: Will פְּדֵנִי retain redemption language or become an immediate request for rescue?
question.background: The verb פּדה concerns release or redemption, including release from danger. This verse specifies neither a payment nor its means. Traditional Christian reception can hear ransom theology here, but that is not separately stated in the Hebrew.

options.choice: Retain redeem.
options.effect: Preserves the traditional term and release associations; may evoke a developed theological account or imply a payment.

options.choice: Use rescue or deliver.
options.held_by: NET uses rescue; Brenton uses redeem in his psalm text, while Augustine’s exposition discusses deliverance.
options.effect: Makes the immediate plea clear and can ease the meter; reduces the distinctive redemption vocabulary.

annotations.answer: Retain redeem.

question.question: Will וְחָנֵּנִי ask for gracious favor or mercy?
question.background: The root חנן asks for favor freely shown to someone in need. Mercy is an established contextual rendering, but modern English can make it chiefly a request for forgiveness of wrongdoing. The verse itself does not confess a particular offense.

options.choice: Ask God to be gracious or show favor.
options.effect: Preserves the appeal to freely given help; gracious can sound formal or merely courteous.

options.choice: Ask God to have mercy.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB, and the Greek tradition.
options.effect: Retains familiar prayer language and emotional urgency; may lead readers to hear an unstated confession of guilt.

annotations.answer: Ask God to have mercy.

question.question: Will the closing footing remain a physical image, become explicit safety, or emphasize uprightness?
question.background: רַגְלִי עָמְדָה בְמִישׁוֹר describes the speaker’s foot as standing on level ground. מִישׁוֹר can also carry associations of straightness or equity; the Greek uses uprightness language. The completed-form verb can describe a presently established position. English may retain singular foot, use feet idiomatically, or speak of footing.

options.choice: Keep the foot or feet standing on level ground.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB; NIV uses plural feet.
options.effect: Preserves the image and answer to possible slipping in verse 1; leaves safety and moral straightness implicit.

options.choice: State that the speaker is secure or safe.
options.effect: Makes the assurance immediately clear; loses the foot and ground imagery.

options.choice: Make uprightness prominent.
options.held_by: The Septuagint’s wording and Augustine’s moral interpretation.
options.effect: Echoes the ethical claim of integrity; can weaken the sense of protection from falling.

annotations.answer: Keep the foot or feet standing on level ground.

question.question: Will you retain the contrast between an evil assembly and worshiping assemblies, including the final plural?
question.background: Verse 5 has קְהַל, an assembly; verse 12 has בְּמַקְהֵלִים, in assemblies, from the same root. Some English versions retain the plural; others express a single great congregation or the worshipers themselves. Great is not separately written in the Masoretic phrase.

options.choice: Use related assembly terms in both verses and retain the final plural.
options.effect: Preserves the word-family echo and repeated public worship; plural assemblies can sound institutional or geographically dispersed.

options.choice: Describe evil company in verse 5 and a single congregation in verse 12.
options.effect: Creates a readily imagined contrast in belonging; obscures the shared root and interprets the Hebrew plural collectively.

options.choice: Refer directly to worshipers or God’s gathered people.
options.effect: Clarifies who participates and can suit a shorter line; replaces the gathering noun and its lexical echo.

annotations.answer: Refer directly to worshipers or God’s gathered people.

question.question: Will the final line bless YHWH in the third person or address God directly in praise?
question.background: The Masoretic אֲבָרֵךְ יְהוָה has YHWH as the object of blessing, without a second-person pronoun. The Septuagint includes an explicit you and treats Lord as an address. English bless can preserve the traditional verb, while praise makes its human-to-God function clearer.

options.choice: Retain a promise to bless YHWH.
options.effect: Preserves the Hebrew construction and traditional worship verb; modern listeners may associate blessing chiefly with receiving benefits.

options.choice: Use praise with YHWH as its object.
options.effect: Clarifies the act of worship; loses the distinctive blessing vocabulary.

options.choice: Address God directly with a promise to bless or praise you.
options.held_by: Septuagint and Brenton retain direct address; CEV also closes by addressing God.
options.effect: Maintains direct prayer through the final words; follows the Greek construction rather than the Masoretic wording.

annotations.answer: Retain a promise to bless YHWH.
